relearning.title: Read: matter, changes and density
relearning.description: A short reading with the school-lunch analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can sort matter into groups (elements, compounds, mixtures), identify physical changes from chemical changes, and use density to figure out what a substance is.**

**Think of a school lunch.** A single grape is like an **element**: one kind of thing. A baked cake is like a **compound**: the flour, eggs and sugar changed into something new that you can't just pick apart. A tray with fries, an apple and milk is a **mixture**: the parts just sit together, and you can separate them.

**Sorting matter.** **Matter** is anything that has mass and takes up space. A **pure substance** is an **element** (only one type of atom, like copper, Cu) or a **compound** (two or more different elements chemically bonded, like H₂O). A **mixture** is two or more substances physically mixed, not bonded. A **homogeneous** mixture is the same all the way through, like salt water (a **solution**). A **heterogeneous** mixture is uneven, and you can see the parts, like vegetable soup.

**Physical vs. chemical change.** A **physical change** does not change what the substance is: melting, cutting, crushing, dissolving. In a **chemical change**, a **new substance** forms: burning, rusting, baking.

**Density** is the amount of mass per unit of volume: **D = m/v**. Each substance has its own density, so density can identify a substance.

**Worked example:** Butter melts in a pan and then burns. Melting is a phase change, and it is still butter, so it is **physical**. Burning makes black smoke and new substances, so it is **chemical**.

checks.prompt: Which of these is a compound?
checks.explanation: CO₂ is two different elements, carbon and oxygen, chemically bonded. O₂ has only one type of atom, so it is an element, even with the 2. Salt water is a mixture. Calling O₂ a compound is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Which of these is a chemical change?
checks.explanation: Burning makes new substances (smoke, ash and gases). Melting and dissolving are physical: it is still water, and it is still sugar. Calling dissolving a chemical change is the common mistake.

sections.title: Signs of change and density

body.text:
**More mixtures.** A **suspension** has large particles that settle over time and can be filtered out, like sand stirred into water. A **colloid** has medium-sized particles that do not settle, like fog.

**The 5 signs of a chemical change:** color change, precipitation (a solid forms), gas production, temperature change, and changes in characteristic properties (like odor or light). Add the word **unpredicted** to each one. Mixing paint, shaking a soda and boiling water show color, bubbles or heat, but no new substance forms, so they are physical changes.

**Using density.** D = m/v, in g/mL or g/cm³ (1 mL = 1 cm³). Water is 1.00 g/mL. Less dense objects float in water, and more dense objects sink. Mass changes with sample size, but density does not. Find volume by **water displacement** (record, drop, record, subtract) or by **L × W × H** for a box shape.

**Worked example 2:** A metal sample has a mass of 82.8 g. It raises the water in a cylinder from 40.0 mL to 52.0 mL. Volume = 52.0 − 40.0 = 12.0 mL = 12.0 cm³. D = 82.8 g ÷ 12.0 cm³ = **6.90 g/cm³**. Zinc is 6.90 g/cm³, so the sample is zinc.

**Worked example 3:** A liquid has a density of 1.18 g/mL. What is the mass of 750.0 mL? m = D × v = 1.18 g/mL × 750.0 mL = **885 g**. The mL cancel, leaving grams.

**Watch out for:** flipping the formula to v/m, using the final water level instead of the change, calling every bubble or color change chemical, and calling a compound like water a mixture.

checks.prompt: A rock has a mass of 31.2 g. It raises the water in a graduated cylinder from 25.0 mL to 37.0 mL. What is its density in g/cm³? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Volume = 37.0 − 25.0 = 12.0 mL = 12.0 cm³. D = 31.2 g ÷ 12.0 cm³ = 2.60 g/cm³. Dividing by the final level (37.0) instead of the change is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A student drops red food coloring into a glass of water, and the water turns red. Which statement is best?

options.text: Chemical change, because the color changed
Physical change, because the color change was predicted and no new substance formed
Chemical change, because a new red substance formed

checks.explanation: The food coloring just mixes with the water, and you expected the red color. The signs only count when they are unpredicted. Calling every color change chemical is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: Hot chocolate powder stirred into hot milk seems to disappear. Is this a physical or a chemical change? Use the words "new substance" or "unpredicted" in your answer.

relearning.title: Do: flip the terms, then find the mystery metal
relearning.description: Flashcards with a 3-question self-quiz, then a density problem one step at a time.

cards.back: A pure substance with only one type of atom, like copper (Cu). It can't be broken down by chemical means.
Two or more different elements chemically bonded, like water (H₂O).
The same all the way through, like salt water. A solution is this kind of mixture.
Uneven. You can see the different parts, like vegetable soup.
Does not change what the substance is: melting, cutting, crushing, dissolving.
A new substance forms: burning, rusting, baking.
Mass per unit of volume: D = m/v, in g/mL or g/cm³. Water is 1.00 g/mL.

checks.prompt: Sweet tea (sugar dissolved in tea, no ice) is a:
checks.explanation: The sugar dissolves and spreads evenly, so sweet tea is the same all the way through: a homogeneous mixture (a solution). The sugar and tea are not chemically bonded, so it is not a compound. Calling a solution a compound is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Which of these is a physical change?
checks.explanation: Crushing changes the can's shape, but it is still aluminum. Toasting and rusting make new substances. Thinking any big change must be chemical is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A wood block has a density of 0.60 g/cm³. What happens when it is placed in water (1.00 g/mL)?

options.text: It floats only if the block is small

checks.explanation: 0.60 is less than 1.00, so the wood is less dense than water and floats. Density doesn't depend on size, so a big block and a small block of the same wood both float. Thinking size matters is the common mistake.

body.problem: A shiny metal nugget has a mass of 124.8 g. When it is dropped into a graduated cylinder, the water rises from 30.0 mL to 42.0 mL. Which metal is it? Density table (g/cm³): aluminum 2.70, zinc 6.90, iron 7.80, copper 8.63, silver 10.40.

steps.text: Find the volume by water displacement: 42.0 mL − 30.0 mL = 12.0 mL. Use the change, not the final level.
Change units: 1 mL = 1 cm³, so the volume is 12.0 cm³.
Use D = m/v: 124.8 g ÷ 12.0 cm³ = 10.4 g/cm³.
Compare to the table: 10.4 g/cm³ matches silver (10.40). The nugget is silver.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a stone has a mass of 30.0 g and raises the water from 18.5 mL to 26.0 mL. What is its density in g/cm³? Type a number.
checks.explanation: Volume = 26.0 − 18.5 = 7.5 cm³. D = 30.0 g ÷ 7.5 cm³ = 4.0 g/cm³. Using 26.0 (the final level) as the volume, or flipping the formula to v/m, is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a metal bar is 4.00 cm long, 2.50 cm wide and 1.00 cm high, with a mass of 78.0 g. Using the same table, what is it?
checks.explanation: Volume = L × W × H = 4.00 × 2.50 × 1.00 = 10.0 cm³. D = 78.0 g ÷ 10.0 cm³ = 7.80 g/cm³, which matches iron. Comparing the mass to the table without finding the density is the common mistake.
